newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Karadzic opponents condemn beating of Serb judge.
newsitem.headline: Karadzic opponents condemn beating of Serb judge.

text.p: Bosnian Serb opposition leaders on Sunday condemned the beating of a constitutional court judge and said it showed that nationalist hardliners were desperate to hold on to the reins of power in Serb-controlled territory.

Independent Serb media reported that Justice Jovo Rosic was badly beaten last Thursday because he opposed plans for the court to strike down a decision by the Bosnian Serb president to dissolve parliament and call early elections.
Rosic was concussed and spent the weekend in hospital in Banja Luka, where soldiers loyal to President Biljana Plavsic guarded his room, Serb media said.
With Rosic absent from the seven-member court, the remaining judges declared Plavsic's move unconstitutional last Friday but gave no explanation for the ruling.
Serb hardliners loyal to ex-president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic pushed through the court decision in a bid to gain the upper hand in their power struggle with Plavsic.

"This is a sign that the SDS (ruling party) has no more political arguments left and must start applying physical repression," Miodrag Zivanovic, leader of the opposition Social Liberal Party, told Reuters by telephone from Banja Luka in northwest Bosnia.
Zivanovic said that the court decision exacerbated the political crisis in Bosnia's Serb republic and threatened to produce two rival authorities, one led by Plavsic and another by Karadzic's allies.
Another opposition leader, Milorad Dodik, said that the court decision was clearly the result of political intimidation and added Plavsic and allied opposition parties would ignore the ruling.
Dodik said that opponents of the hardliners would press ahead with plans to hold early elections in Serb territory which Plavsic has tentatively scheduled for mid-October.
Karadzic's Serb Democratic Party (SDS) suffered a setback over the weekend when several prominent members resigned from the party in Banja Luka, which has become Plavsic's power base.
Plavsic was sacked from the SDS and has announced the formation of her own party which is expected to attract disillusioned members of the SDS.

Plavsic broke with fellow nationalists in Karadzic's party because she says they have betrayed Serb interests by running smuggling rackets and blocking international efforts to enforce a 1995 peace treaty.
The international High Representative to Bosnia, Carlos Westendorp, has dismissed the court ruling and called for holding early elections to resolve the political turmoil.
Bosnian Serb hardliners refused a request on Saturday by Westendorp's deputy, German diplomat Gerd Wagner, to appear on official television to discuss the current crisis.
The United States has led a Western campaign of support for Plavsic in hopes of weakening Karadzic and his allies who they accuse of trying to sabotage the country's peace agreement.
Washington has sought to pile pressure on Karadzic who has clung to power and refused to face trial before the U.N. war crimes tribunal.

NATO and senior U.S. officials have warned that Karadzic will not be allowed to pull strings behind the scenes indefinitely. British soldiers pounced on two Serbs suspected of war crimes last month and NATO has refused to rule out the possibility of further arrest operations.
